register: wave-5 authoring register (S-B5 tranche) — part 1 of 2

items.stem: State the two substances that must both be present for iron to rust.
items.modelAnswer: Both oxygen and water must be present for iron to rust; either one on its own is not enough.

items.stem: What job does the calcium chloride do in the dry test tube of the rusting experiment?
items.modelAnswer: Calcium chloride is a drying agent: it absorbs water molecules, keeping the air in that tube dry.

items.stem: Explain why only one of the three nails rusts in the classic three-tube experiment.
items.modelAnswer: Only the nail with both air and water can rust. The boiled-water tube has no dissolved oxygen left, and the drying agent keeps the dry tube free of water, so each control lacks one of the two substances rusting needs.

items.stem: An iron gate is scratched down to the metal on a rainy day. Use the rusting conditions and the nature of rust to describe what will happen to the scratch over time.
items.modelAnswer: Water from the rain and oxygen from the air are both present at the scratch, so the exposed iron rusts. The rust flakes off easily, exposing fresh iron underneath, so the corrosion keeps going and the gate weakens over time.

items.stem: Name the common barrier methods listed for protecting iron from rusting.
items.modelAnswer: Paint, oil, grease and electroplating are the common barrier methods named in the note.

items.stem: How exactly do barriers stop iron from rusting?
items.modelAnswer: A barrier keeps water and oxygen away from the iron, so the two substances needed for rust never reach the metal.

items.stem: Explain why a scratched barrier can be more damaging than it first appears.
items.modelAnswer: Once the coating is broken the iron is exposed and rusts again. Because rust is porous it does not seal the surface, so corrosion continues internally underneath and the damage spreads.

items.stem: Some metals used outdoors never need painting, unlike iron railings. Use this lesson's comparison to explain why their surfaces stay sound once formed.
items.modelAnswer: Unlike iron, some other metals form protective layers that do not flake away, so the surface stays sealed and the metal underneath is protected; iron's rust is porous and flakes, so it never protects the metal below it.

items.stem: Describe how sacrificial protection keeps a piece of iron safe.
items.modelAnswer: A more reactive metal is attached to the iron; that metal oxidises and corrodes first, so it is sacrificed while the iron itself is protected.

items.stem: What maintenance do the zinc bars on a steel ship need, and why must it be done in time?
items.modelAnswer: The zinc bars must be replaced before they completely corrode, because the zinc sacrifices itself by corroding first; once it is gone the iron would no longer be protected.

items.stem: Zinc blocks are bolted to a steel hull below the waterline. Use electron loss to explain why the zinc corrodes first while the iron behind it survives.
items.modelAnswer: Zinc loses its electrons more easily than iron, so zinc is oxidised more easily and corrodes first; the zinc gives up its electrons in place of the iron and keeps the iron intact.

items.stem: Scratch a galvanised dustbin deeply and leave it out in the rain: the iron at the scratch still stays rust-free. Give the two ways the zinc continues to protect the damaged spot.
items.modelAnswer: The surrounding zinc coating still keeps water and oxygen away from the scratch as a barrier, and zinc carbonate (ZnCO3) forms when the zinc meets the air to strengthen that barrier; in addition the zinc in contact with the iron acts sacrificially, corroding before the iron does.

items.stem: Name three greenhouse gases.
items.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are three greenhouse gases.

items.stem: What is the name given to the natural warming of the planet by greenhouse gases?
items.modelAnswer: The natural warming of the planet is known as the greenhouse effect.

items.stem: A student claims the greenhouse effect is purely harmful and should be eliminated. Give the correct verdict and justify it with what the effect does for the planet.
items.modelAnswer: Greenhouse gases keep temperatures on Earth high enough to support life; without this natural warming the planet would be too cold for living things to survive.

items.stem: Trace one parcel of energy: short wavelength radiation from the sun strikes the Earth's surface and is re-emitted. Describe what happens to that re-emitted energy in an atmosphere containing greenhouse gases.
items.modelAnswer: The surface re-emits the energy as long wavelength radiation, and greenhouse gases absorb and store much of it, trapping the energy in the atmosphere so it warms the planet.

items.stem: List two processes that add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
items.modelAnswer: Combustion of wood and fossil fuels, and respiration of plants and animals, both add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.

items.stem: Name the two kinds of carbonate reaction that release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
items.modelAnswer: Carbonate rocks breaking down with heat, and acids acting on carbonates, both free carbon dioxide gas.

items.stem: Carbon dioxide makes up only a tiny share of the air. Use this lesson's trapping law to account for its outsized warming effect.
items.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide and methane are present only in small amounts, yet they trap extra heat energy in the atmosphere, so even a little of these gases has a big warming role.

items.stem: A country burns far more fossil fuel this decade than it did in the last one. State the expected change in its carbon dioxide output and the long-term concern the specification attaches to rising atmospheric carbon dioxide.
items.modelAnswer: Burning more fuel releases more carbon dioxide, so atmospheric carbon dioxide levels rise, and rising carbon dioxide may help drive climate change.

items.stem: Give the two approximate volume percentages that describe dry air, naming the gas each one belongs to.
items.modelAnswer: Nitrogen is about 80 percent (roughly four-fifths) and oxygen about 20 percent (roughly one-fifth) of dry air by volume.

items.stem: List the minor constituents that fill the small remaining share of dry air.
items.modelAnswer: Small proportions of carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases make up the remainder of dry air.

items.stem: Explain why carbon dioxide is described as significant even though it is only a very small part of the air.
items.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide is present only in a very small amount, yet it has a large warming role, so its effect on the atmosphere is far bigger than its share of the air suggests.

items.stem: A sample of dry air sealed today is compared with one trapped in rock 200 million years ago. State what the lesson says about how their compositions should compare and what that tells you about the atmosphere.
items.modelAnswer: The proportion of gases in the air has changed little in 200 million years, so the two samples should be very similar in composition; the atmosphere has stayed remarkably stable over that time.

items.stem: State what happens to the gas volume inside the sealed bell jar as the phosphorus burns, and what that does to the water beneath.
items.modelAnswer: The burning phosphorus consumes the oxygen inside the sealed jar, so the gas volume falls and water rises up the jar to take its place.

items.stem: What property makes phosphorus a suitable reactant for measuring the oxygen content of air?
items.modelAnswer: Phosphorus keeps burning until no oxygen is left, so it uses up all the oxygen in the sealed sample of air.

items.stem: Explain why the air sample in this experiment must be measured and sealed before the reactant is used.
items.modelAnswer: A chosen reactant consumes the oxygen from a measured, sealed sample of air; if the jar leaked or the starting volume were unknown, the rise in water could not be converted into a fair percentage of oxygen.

items.stem: A student proposes leaving the bell jar loosely lidded so more phosphorus can be added part-way through. Predict and explain the effect on the result, naming the safety property of phosphorus that makes care essential.
items.modelAnswer: The jar must stay sealed: a loose lid lets fresh air in, so oxygen keeps being replaced and the final water rise no longer equals the oxygen fraction of the original sample. Phosphorus is also toxic, so careless handling adds real danger.

items.stem: State the colour and physical state of bromine and of iodine at room temperature.
items.modelAnswer: Bromine is a red-brown liquid and iodine is a grey solid at room temperature.

items.stem: What colours do chlorine, bromine and iodine give when dissolved in the aqueous layer?
items.modelAnswer: In solution chlorine appears pale green, bromine orange and iodine dark brown.

items.stem: Explain why the melting and boiling points of the halogens increase on descending Group 7.
items.modelAnswer: The atoms get larger down the group, giving stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to overcome them and the melting and boiling points rise.

items.stem: An unlabelled halogen sample is a dark grey solid at room temperature. Identify the halogen and justify the identification using the colour and state trends of the group.
items.modelAnswer: The sample is iodine: the halogens darken down the group and their melting and boiling points rise, so the dark grey solid, the highest-melting form listed, is iodine rather than the paler gases or the red-brown liquid bromine.

items.stem: Calcium forms CaBr2 with bromine. Use the halide charge to explain why the formula needs two bromide ions.
items.modelAnswer: The halide ion carries a 1- charge, so two bromide ions are needed to balance the 2+ charge of the calcium ion.

items.stem: Compare the conditions fluorine and chlorine each need to react with hydrogen.
items.modelAnswer: Fluorine reacts with hydrogen without light, while chlorine needs light or a high temperature before it will react.

items.stem: Explain why iron is attacked more slowly by bromine and iodine than by chlorine.
items.modelAnswer: Reactivity decreases down Group 7, so bromine and iodine, sitting lower in the group, are less reactive halogens and attack metals such as iron more slowly than chlorine does.

items.stem: A metal ion carries a 3+ charge and forms a salt with chlorine. Write the formula of its chloride and state how many electrons each chlorine atom gains when the salt forms.
items.modelAnswer: The chloride has the formula MCl3: each halide carries a 1- charge, so three chloride ions balance the 3+ metal ion, and each chlorine atom gains one electron to become a chloride ion.

items.stem: State the colour change when chlorine solution is added to colourless potassium bromide solution, and name the substance causing it.
items.modelAnswer: The solution turns orange because bromine is formed as chlorine displaces it from the bromide.

items.stem: Write the symbol equation for chlorine displacing iodine from potassium iodide solution.
items.modelAnswer: Cl2 + 2KI gives 2KCl + I2: the chlorine displaces iodine, forming potassium chloride and iodine.

items.stem: Explain why mixing iodine solution with potassium chloride solution produces no reaction.
items.modelAnswer: Iodine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace chloride from solution; it also cannot displace bromide, and only a more reactive halogen can push a less reactive one out of its salt.

items.stem: A student adds bromine solution to potassium iodide solution in one tube and to potassium chloride solution in another. Predict both outcomes and deduce the reactivity order the results demonstrate.
items.modelAnswer: Bromine displaces iodine from potassium iodide, turning that tube brown, but nothing happens with potassium chloride; this shows bromine can only displace elements below it, so the reactivity order is chlorine, then bromine, then iodine.

items.stem: List the metals of the reactivity series of record in order, from the most reactive to the least reactive.
items.modelAnswer: Potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver and gold, running from the most reactive at the top to the least reactive at the bottom.

items.stem: Where do the non-metals carbon and hydrogen sit in the reactivity series?
items.modelAnswer: Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc, and hydrogen sits between iron and copper.

items.stem: Explain why carbon's position in the reactivity series matters industrially.
items.modelAnswer: Carbon's place between aluminium and zinc decides which metal oxides it can strip oxygen from: it is used to extract metals that sit below it in the series from their oxides.

items.stem: Iron fizzes in dilute acid but copper is untouched by the same acid. Use hydrogen's seat in the series to explain the difference.
items.modelAnswer: Hydrogen sits between iron and copper, so iron lies above hydrogen and can push hydrogen out of the acid, while copper lies below hydrogen and cannot displace it, which is why copper shows no reaction.

items.stem: Which metals do the words lions, cats and monkeys stand for in the mnemonic?
items.modelAnswer: Lions stands for lithium, cats for calcium and monkeys for magnesium.

items.stem: Which two non-metals appear in the mnemonic, and which words mark their rungs?
items.modelAnswer: Carbon appears as the word cute and hydrogen appears as the word hot.

items.stem: Explain how the mnemonic keeps silver and gold in their correct places in the series.
items.modelAnswer: Silver and gold finish the sentence, matching their places at the bottom of the series as the least reactive metals, so the end of the sentence mirrors the end of the series.

items.stem: A student expands the mnemonic's rungs as P, S, L, C, M, A, C, Z, I, H, C, S, G and notices two letters repeat. Name the metals at the repeated rungs and the metals each could be confused with.
items.modelAnswer: C repeats: the first C is cute, which is carbon between aluminium and zinc, and the later C is copper. S repeats: the first S is send, which is sodium, while the final S is silver near the bottom.

items.stem: Compare how potassium and lithium each react with cold water.
items.modelAnswer: Potassium reacts violently with cold water while lithium reacts less strongly, though both react visibly and quickly.

items.stem: Write the balanced equation, and name the products, for calcium reacting with cold water.
items.modelAnswer: Calcium plus water gives calcium hydroxide and hydrogen: Ca + 2H2O gives Ca(OH)2 + H2.

items.stem: Explain how the cold-water and steam reactions together allow magnesium, zinc and iron to be placed in an order of reactivity.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium barely reacts with cold water yet responds rapidly to steam, so it is clearly more reactive than zinc and iron, which react only slowly with steam; the falling vigour from magnesium, to zinc and iron, orders the three metals.

items.stem: Iron wool fizzes slowly in steam while a piece of copper in the same steam shows no change at all. State which metal is more reactive and justify the ranking with this note's ladder.
items.modelAnswer: Iron is more reactive: it reacts with steam, though only slowly, while copper shows no reaction with water or steam at all, so iron must sit above copper in the reactivity series.

items.stem: State the general pattern for the reaction of a metal with dilute acid.
items.modelAnswer: Metal plus acid gives a salt plus hydrogen.

items.stem: Name the salts formed when magnesium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid and with dilute hydrochloric acid.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium sulfate forms with sulfuric acid and magnesium chloride forms with hydrochloric acid.

items.stem: A teacher refuses to generate hydrogen from dilute acid using potassium or sodium. Justify the refusal using this lesson's vigour law.
items.modelAnswer: Potassium and sodium react explosively with acids, so the reaction is far too dangerous to try in school; their very high reactivity makes them unsafe choices.

items.stem: Pieces of magnesium, zinc and copper are dropped into separate tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid. Predict the order of vigour observed and name the metal that shows no reaction at all.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium fizzes most vigorously, zinc reacts more slowly, and copper shows no reaction at all: the vigour follows the reactivity series, and copper lies below hydrogen so it cannot react with dilute acid.
